messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Diego was twenty-two when his younger brother Mateo was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. For eighteen months, he lived in the fluorescent hum of the pediatric oncology ward, watching his brother’s body shrink and swell with steroids, listening to the rhythm of infusion pumps and the occasional shriek of a monitor. He learned to read the sound of a siren before it arrived—first as a distant whine, then a scream that meant blood cultures, platelets, another crisis. He learned the smell of the hospital: antiseptic layered over sweat, over the sour breath of a feverish child, over his own unwashed clothes. He learned that crying meant bad news. When Mateo finally went into remission, Diego thought he could go back to his life. He was wrong.

Now, at twenty-five, Diego works as a data scientist in a downtown office, but he spends most of his day with noise-canceling headphones on, jump-starting at the hum of the HVAC or a dropped pen. The sound of a siren—even blocks away—makes his heart slam against his ribs, his palms slick, his breath shallow. He has come to believe that his body is still on alert, that if he lets his guard down something terrible will happen again. When he smells sweat on the subway—a commuter’s body odor, a runner’s damp shirt—his stomach turns and he feels the same terror he felt the night Mateo spiked a fever and the doctors couldn’t stop the seizure. The memory itself feels unreal, like a story he heard about someone else, and he cannot put the sequence in order: was the seizure before the blood transfusion or after? He only knows the terror, which arrives whole and unannounced. That terror, in turn, makes him scan the street for ambulances, makes him listen for sirens even when there are none, and the more he scans, the more he notices the faintest sounds—a distant wail, a car alarm—and the more he startles.

Diego has learned to manage. He never allows himself to feel or express anger; he has come to believe that anger is dangerous, that it might break the fragile peace he has built. When a coworker snaps at him in a meeting, Diego feels the heat rise in his chest and immediately pushes it down, telling himself it’s nothing. He tries hard not to think about the trauma at all. He avoids hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations—he hasn’t seen a doctor in two years, not even for a cold, because the smell of antiseptic and the sight of a stethoscope bring back the confusion and the terror. But the effort of suppression has a cost. When he pushes a memory away, it returns later, more fragmented, more unreal, and the next time he hears a siren or smells sweat, the memory feels even more extreme, harder to believe it really happened. The effort also keeps him vigilant: he cannot fall asleep easily because he feels he needs to stay alert, listening for the sound that might mean crisis. And his constant vigilance makes him even more sensitive to triggers. He has started to avoid crowded places where he might smell sweat; he has stopped going to the gym; he has stopped taking the subway, spending extra money on ride-shares where he can control the windows.

His avoidance has cost him. His manager has noticed his absences from team lunches and his refusal to attend the office health fair. Diego has stopped dating because he cannot explain why he panics when a partner cries during a movie. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week: a siren passed his apartment at 3 a.m., and he spent the next hour on his hands and knees, gasping, certain that Mateo was dying again, even though Mateo is healthy and asleep in his own bed across town. Diego is terrified that he is losing his mind. He is hoping that someone can help him make the terror stop—or at least help him understand why his own body has become the thing he cannot escape.
